newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN worried over 150 Rwanda Hutu returnees arrested.
newsitem.headline: UN worried over 150 Rwanda Hutu returnees arrested.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency expressed concern on Friday over reports that at least 150 Rwandan Hutu returnees from Tanzania had been arrested in their villages, based on neighbours' suspicion of their role in the 1994 genocide.

UNHCR spokeswoman Pamela O'Toole, citing reports from Murambi and Nyagatare in northeastern Rwanda, said returnees had been arrested in the last few days on the basis of accusations levelled by other villagers.

"We've heard reports that on returning to their communes in some areas, people are being arrested as suspected genocide perpetrators on the basis of accusations levelled by individual members of the public," O'Toole told a news briefing in Geneva.
"We are raising this issue with the Rwandan government and pointing out that Rwandan law stipulates that any arrest should only be carried out in accordance with proper legal procedures.
"Under Rwandan law, a warrant should be issued on the basis of a prepared file before someone is arrested," she added.
Few of the 90,000 Hutu genocide suspects crammed into overcrowded jails have case files and officials have forgotton when many were arrested, where and by whom.
Rwanda has yet to pass legislation on genocide crimes and trials have been repeatedly delayed.
Some 800 Hutus are being arrested every week on genocide accusations by survivor Tutsis in Rwanda, U.N. officials and diplomats say.
O'Toole said it was not clear whether the returnees might have been taken into custody "for their own protection".
"In this area, people have a tendency to take the law into their own hands. Those identified by the public could be in severe risk if they weren't taken into custody by the local authorities."
More than 800,000 refugees from Zaire and Tanzania have returned to Rwanda in the past five weeks. Almost one in six Rwandans is a recently returned refugee.
More than two million Hutus fled Rwanda in fear of reprisals for the genocide of more than half a million minority Tutsis and Hutu moderates, after which a Tutsi-led army swept to power.
UNHCR understood that passions were running high in areas where massacres were perpetrated, according to the spokeswoman.
"But it is obviously important that this is contained by the proper legal process," she said.
